content: Malaria is a disease caused by a parasite. The parasite is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes. Symptoms of malaria typically appear within 7 to 30 days after infection, but in some cases, they may take up to a year to develop. Common symptoms include high fevers, shaking chills, and flu-like illness. If left untreated, malaria can lead to severe illness and even death. The mosquitoes that transmit malaria are found in regions such as Africa, Central and South America, parts of the Caribbean, Asia, Eastern Europe, and the South Pacific. Travelers visiting these areas are at risk of being bitten by infected mosquitoes and contracting malaria. In the United States, approximately 2,000 cases of malaria are diagnosed annually, primarily among travelers returning from these regions. To prevent malaria, travelers should take prescription medications and take measures to avoid mosquito bites. Currently, there is no vaccine available for malaria. It is important to check the destination-specific recommendations to determine if malaria prophylaxis is necessary. Depending on the medication prescribed, travelers may need to start taking it several days before their trip, continue during their stay, and for a period after returning. To prevent mosquito bites, travelers should use insect repellents that are registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and contain active ingredients such as DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE). These repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women. If sunscreen is also being used, insect repellent should be applied after sunscreen. For babies and children, additional precautions should be taken. Dress them in clothing that covers their arms and legs, and use mosquito netting over strollers and baby carriers. When applying insect repellent to children, follow label instructions carefully. Avoid using products containing OLE or para-menthane-diol (PMD) on children under 3 years old. Do not apply repellent to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, cuts, or irritated skin. Adults should spray repellent onto their hands first and then apply it to the child’s face. Always apply insect repellent after sunscreen if both are being used. Permethrin, an insecticide that kills or repels mosquitoes and other insects, can be used to treat clothing and gear such as boots, pants, socks, and tents. Alternatively, travelers can purchase pre-treated clothing and gear. Permethrin-treated items remain effective after multiple washes, but it is important to follow product instructions to determine the duration of protection. Permethrin should never be applied directly to the skin. To keep mosquitoes out of sleeping areas, choose accommodations with air conditioning or window and door screens. If these are not available, or if sleeping outdoors, use a mosquito net. Mosquito nets should be compact, white, rectangular, and have 156 holes per square inch. They should also be long enough to tuck under the mattress. Treated mosquito nets provide additional protection compared to untreated ones. If washing a treated net, follow the label instructions to ensure its effectiveness is maintained. If bitten by mosquitoes, avoid scratching the bites. To relieve itching, apply over-the-counter anti-itch or antihistamine creams.
